# The Science of a Good Loaf

Great bread is a small set of processes happening in the same bowl: starches
hydrating, proteins linking into gluten, yeasts producing gas, and heat
finally setting the crumb. Understanding each process in isolation makes most
recipes legible, because nearly every instruction in a bread recipe exists to
favour one of these processes over another.

## Flour, water and time

Wheat flour carries two storage proteins, glutenin and gliadin. When water is
added and the flour rests, they unwind and begin to bond into an elastic
network. Given time and gentle handling that network develops on its own,
which is why a long rest can replace much of the hard kneading a recipe asks
for.

Enzymes in the flour, mainly amylase, slowly cut starches into sugars. Those
sugars feed the yeast and, later, sweeten the crust through browning. A dough
that rests longer tastes faintly sweeter and browns deeper for exactly this
reason.

## Gas, structure and heat

Fermentation produces carbon dioxide that collects inside the gluten
network. In the oven the gas expands, the loaf springs upward, and heat sets
the crumb, turning a soft paste into a sliceable structure. The baker's job
is less about forcing any of this and more about timing it.

## Ratios

Professional bakers describe every formula as a set of percentages of the
flour weight. Writing a recipe that way makes hydration explicit and lets a
baker scale the formula to any amount of flour without arithmetic surprises.
